questions.stem: A 25 year old man with sickle cell disease has severe pain in his lower back and thighs for 8 hours. It began after an evening swim in a cold lake. His temperature is 37.1°C, pulse rate 104 bpm, BP 128/76 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. His chest is clear and there is no splenomegaly. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Severe pain after a cold trigger with a normal examination and Hb at baseline is a vaso-occlusive crisis; aplastic crisis would show a falling Hb with a low reticulocyte count.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: His chest is clear and there is no splenomegaly
severe pain in his lower back and thighs
steps.x: Cold trigger, pain, normal examination and no significant Hb drop.

elim: Chest is clear and saturations are normal; no chest pain or infiltrate.
Would cause a big fall in Hb with a LOW reticulocyte count.
Would cause a significant drop in Hb with worsening jaundice.
A crisis of young children with an enlarging spleen and shock.

steps.x: **E. Vaso-occlusive crisis.** Pain + normal examination + Hb at baseline = vaso-occlusive crisis.

questions.stem: A 29 year old man whose parents are from Ghana has had episodes of yellow eyes since childhood. His brother needs regular blood transfusions for 'a blood problem'. Ultrasound shows multiple gallstones. He has no splenomegaly. Blood film shows sickled red cells and Howell-Jolly bodies. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Lifelong normocytic haemolytic anaemia with gallstones, African ancestry, an affected sibling and sickled cells with Howell-Jolly bodies (hyposplenism) is sickle cell disease.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: His brother needs regular blood transfusions
steps.x: Ancestry, family history, chronic haemolysis (jaundice, pigment stones) and signs of hyposplenism.

elim: Acquired; would not explain a lifelong course, family history and sickled cells.
Causes a microcytic anaemia; the MCV here is normal.
Episodic haemolysis after oxidant triggers, with bite cells and Heinz bodies.
Spherocytes and splenomegaly, not sickled cells and hyposplenism.

steps.x: **E. Sickle cell disease.** Normocytic haemolysis + gallstones + Howell-Jolly bodies in a patient of African ancestry = sickle cell disease.

questions.stem: A 34 year old woman with sickle cell disease attends haematology clinic for review. She has had many painful crises since childhood and an ultrasound in childhood showed a small spleen. She is well today. Her full blood count shows a normocytic anaemia and raised reticulocyte count. A blood film is examined.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on her blood film?
questions.e: Repeated splenic infarction leaves her hyposplenic, so nuclear remnants are not removed from red cells: Howell-Jolly bodies.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Repeated infarction has shrunk the spleen: functional hyposplenism.

elim: Seen in G6PD deficiency after oxidant damage.
Denatured haemoglobin in G6PD deficiency.
A feature of B12 or folate deficiency (megaloblastic anaemia).
Hereditary spherocytosis or autoimmune haemolysis.

steps.x: **C. Howell-Jolly bodies.** Hyposplenism in sickle cell disease shows Howell-Jolly bodies on the film.

questions.stem: A 15 year old boy with sickle cell disease was admitted 2 days ago with pain in both legs and treated with morphine. He now has a fever, pleuritic chest pain, cough and wheeze. His temperature is 38.4°C, pulse rate 118 bpm, respiratory rate 30 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 90% breathing air. There are crackles and bronchial breathing at both bases. Chest X-ray (see item resources).
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Fever, chest pain, tachypnoea, wheeze and new pulmonary infiltrates starting at the bases in a patient with sickle cell disease define acute chest syndrome.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: admitted 2 days ago with pain in both legs
crackles and bronchial breathing at both bases
steps.x: A vaso-occlusive crisis evolving into hypoxia with new basal consolidation.

elim: Would show a lung edge with absent markings, not basal infiltrates.
Does not cause bilateral basal consolidation, fever and bronchial breathing.
No fluid overload history; would show a bat-wing pattern without fever.
Would not cause hypoxia, fever and new infiltrates.

steps.x: **A. Acute chest syndrome.** Sickle cell + chest symptoms + new infiltrate = acute chest syndrome.

questions.stem: A 30 year old woman with sickle cell disease stopped taking her daily antibiotic tablets a year ago. She has had a headache, vomiting and a fever for 12 hours. Her temperature is 39.4°C, pulse rate 124 bpm and BP 88/50 mmHg. She has neck stiffness and a non-blanching purpuric rash on her legs.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Functional asplenia leaves her at risk of encapsulated organisms; meningitis with a non-blanching purpuric rash is meningococcal.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: stopped taking her daily antibiotic tablets
steps.x: Hyposplenic patient off penicillin prophylaxis with meningitis and purpura.

elim: A cause of neonatal meningitis and urinary sepsis, not purpuric meningitis here.
Meningitis in neonates, the elderly and pregnancy; no purpuric rash.
Not an encapsulated organism linked to asplenia; does not cause meningococcal rash.
Group B streptococcus causes neonatal sepsis.

steps.x: **C. Neisseria meningitidis.** Asplenia: S. pneumoniae, H. influenzae, N. meningitidis. Purpuric rash = meningococcus.

questions.stem: A 6 year old boy with sickle cell disease has been pale and tired for 3 days. His class at school had an outbreak of 'slapped cheek' illness. His pulse rate is 140 bpm and respiratory rate 32 breaths per minute. There is no splenomegaly. Investigations are shown.

visual.title: Haemoglobin and reticulocytes
visual.caption: Hb falls as the reticulocyte count collapses.

questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Parvovirus B19 ('slapped cheek') infects red cell precursors, so Hb falls with a very low reticulocyte count: aplastic crisis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Severe anaemia, low reticulocytes, no splenomegaly, slapped cheek contacts.

elim: Causes congenital infection and disease in the immunosuppressed, not red cell aplasia here.
Causes infectious mononucleosis with sore throat and lymphadenopathy.
Causes roseola infantum.
Causes a maculopapular rash with cough, coryza and conjunctivitis.

steps.x: **E. Parvovirus B19.** Aplastic crisis = parvovirus B19: Hb down, reticulocytes down.

questions.stem: A 2 year old girl with sickle cell disease becomes suddenly pale and sleepy over 4 hours and holds her tummy. Her pulse rate is 176 bpm, BP 66/40 mmHg and capillary refill time 4 seconds. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely finding on examination of her abdomen?
o: Generalised guarding with absent bowel sounds
Right upper quadrant tenderness with positive Murphy's sign
questions.e: Splenic sequestration traps blood in the spleen: sudden anaemia and shock with a raised reticulocyte count and an enlarging spleen.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.
Young child, acute anaemia with shock, high reticulocytes (marrow working).

elim: Not a feature of sickle crises.
Suggests peritonitis or perforation.
Acute cholecystitis, which does not cause sudden severe anaemia and shock.
Suggests bowel obstruction.

steps.x: **A. Enlarged spleen.** Splenic sequestration: Hb down, reticulocytes UP, spleen big, shocked child.

questions.stem: A 7 year old boy with sickle cell disease suddenly cannot lift his right arm and his speech is slurred. His mother noticed it 1 hour ago while he was eating. His temperature is 36.9°C, pulse rate 98 bpm and BP 108/66 mmHg. Capillary glucose is 5.6 mmol/L. He has right facial droop and right arm weakness.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: Children with sickle cell disease are at particular risk of ischaemic stroke from cerebral vaso-occlusion; sudden focal weakness with normal glucose is a stroke.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: suddenly cannot lift his right arm
steps.x: Sudden focal deficit in a child with sickle cell disease.

elim: No fever, headache or neck stiffness.
Lower motor neurone facial weakness alone; does not cause arm weakness or dysarthria.
Capillary glucose is normal.
Follows a seizure; none was seen.

steps.x: **D. Ischaemic stroke.** Sickle cell + sudden focal neurology, especially in a child = stroke.

questions.stem: A 36 year old man with sickle cell disease has had pain in his left groin for 2 months. It is worse when walking and now wakes him at night. He has no fever. He walks with a limp and internal rotation of the left hip is painful and reduced. A hip X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Avascular necrosis of the femoral head
questions.e: Repeated vaso-occlusion infarcts the femoral head; early avascular necrosis can be invisible on X-ray and is detected on MRI.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: internal rotation of the left hip is painful and reduced
steps.x: Gradual hip pain in sickle cell disease with an early normal X-ray.

elim: Would give a groin lump with a cough impulse, not painful hip rotation.
Unusual at 36 and would usually show changes on X-ray.
Acute, with fever and an inability to move the joint.
Lateral hip pain with tenderness over the greater trochanter; hip rotation is preserved.

steps.x: **A. Avascular necrosis of the femoral head.** Sickle cell + hip pain = avascular necrosis until proven otherwise.

questions.stem: An 18 year old woman with sickle cell disease had a febrile viral illness a week ago. She now has worsening yellow eyes, dark urine and tiredness. Her pulse rate is 112 bpm. There is no splenomegaly and her chest is clear. Investigations are shown.
questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
questions.e: A significant fall in Hb with deepening jaundice and a brisk reticulocyte response after an infection is a haemolytic crisis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: febrile viral illness a week ago
steps.x: Infection, then a big Hb drop with jaundice, high reticulocytes and no splenomegaly.

elim: No chest symptoms and the chest is clear.
Reticulocytes would be low, not high.
The spleen would be enlarged; mainly in young children.
Causes pain without a significant fall in Hb.

steps.x: **C. Haemolytic crisis.** Hb down + jaundice up + reticulocytes up = haemolytic crisis.

questions.stem: A 10 year old girl with sickle cell disease has had a fever and a painful, swollen right forearm for 6 days despite regular analgesia. Her temperature is 39.0°C. Investigations: CRP 186 mg/L (<5). X-ray shows periosteal reaction of the radius. Blood cultures grow Gram-negative bacilli that do not ferment lactose.
questions.q: Which is the most likely causative organism?
questions.e: Osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease is classically Salmonella, a non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus; Staphylococcus aureus is Gram-positive.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: Gram-negative bacilli that do not ferment lactose
steps.x: Osteomyelitis in sickle cell disease with a non-lactose-fermenting Gram-negative bacillus.

elim: A Gram-negative bacillus, but it ferments lactose.
A Gram-negative coccobacillus; not the classic sickle osteomyelitis organism.
The commonest cause of osteomyelitis overall, but a Gram-positive coccus.
A Gram-positive coccus.

steps.x: **C. Salmonella species.** Sickle cell osteomyelitis = Salmonella.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man with sickle cell disease has had constant right upper quadrant pain and fever for 2 days. He is tender in the right upper quadrant and stops breathing in on palpation there. His temperature is 38.3°C and pulse rate 106 bpm. Investigations: WCC 16.2 ×10⁹/L (4–11), bilirubin 64 µmol/L (<21), ALT 38 U/L (<40).

visual.title: Site of pain
visual.caption: Right upper quadrant tenderness with Murphy's sign.

questions.q: Which is the most likely diagnosis?
o: Right lower lobe acute chest syndrome
questions.e: Chronic haemolysis forms pigment gallstones, and sickling and sludging can cause gallbladder ischaemia: RUQ pain, fever and Murphy's sign is acute cholecystitis.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: stops breathing in on palpation there
right upper quadrant pain and fever
steps.x: Murphy's sign with fever and a raised white cell count.

elim: Pain would settle in the right iliac fossa.
Epigastric pain radiating to the back.
No cough, hypoxia or chest signs.
ALT would be markedly raised; Murphy's sign suggests the gallbladder.

steps.x: **B. Acute cholecystitis.** Sickle cell + RUQ pain + fever + Murphy's sign = acute cholecystitis.

questions.stem: A 27 year old woman with sickle cell disease has severe pain in her arms and chest wall for 6 hours. Three days ago she developed a sore throat and fever that is still present. She has been drinking normally and her flat is warm. She has not travelled or exercised. Her temperature is 38.2°C. Examination shows a red throat and is otherwise normal.
questions.q: Which is the most likely trigger of her crisis?
questions.e: Infection is a common trigger of sickling; her fever and sore throat preceded the painful crisis and the other triggers are excluded by the history.

steps.x: A diagnosis-type question: name the pattern yourself before looking at the options.

clues: sore throat and fever that is still present
steps.x: Infection came first; cold, dehydration and altitude are absent.

elim: Her flat is warm.
She has been drinking normally.
She has not travelled.
She has not exercised.

steps.x: **D. Infection.** Triggers of sickling: infection, dehydration, hypoxia, cold, acidosis. Always treat the trigger.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy who recently moved to the UK from Nigeria has had recurrent episodes of severe bone pain since early childhood. He has never had a blood test. Examination shows mild scleral icterus. Investigations: Hb 86 g/L (130–180), MCV 87 fL (80–100), reticulocytes 7% (0.5–2.5). A blood film shows sickle-shaped red cells.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate investigation to confirm the diagnosis?
questions.e: Haemoglobin electrophoresis detects HbS and is the gold standard for confirming sickle cell disease.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.

clues: recurrent episodes of severe bone pain
steps.x: A suspected haemoglobinopathy needs the haemoglobin type identified.

elim: Invasive and does not identify the abnormal haemoglobin.
Detects autoimmune haemolysis.
Used for hereditary spherocytosis.
Assesses iron stores, not haemoglobin type.

steps.x: **C. Haemoglobin electrophoresis.** Confirm sickle cell disease with haemoglobin electrophoresis (HbS).

questions.stem: A 24 year old man with known sickle cell disease (HbSS) comes to the Emergency Department feeling exhausted and breathless on stairs for 2 days. His eyes look more yellow than usual. He has no pain. His pulse rate is 110 bpm, respiratory rate 20 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. His chest is clear.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
o: Full blood count, reticulocyte count and haemolysis screen
questions.e: Possible worsening anaemia with jaundice needs FBC, reticulocyte count and a haemolysis screen (bilirubin, LDH) to separate haemolytic from aplastic crisis.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.
Symptomatic anaemia with jaundice in known sickle cell disease.

elim: Not a first-line test; only if marrow failure is unexplained.
He is not hypoxic and the picture is of worsening anaemia.
His diagnosis is already known; it will not explain this episode.
Jaundice here is haemolytic; first measure the Hb and the haemolysis.

steps.x: **C. Full blood count, reticulocyte count and haemolysis screen.** First-line in a sickle crisis with anaemia: FBC, reticulocytes, haemolysis screen.

questions.stem: A 21 year old woman with sickle cell disease comes to the Emergency Department with pain in her knees and lower back, typical of her usual painful crises. Her temperature is 37.0°C, pulse rate 100 bpm, BP 118/72 mmHg and oxygen saturation 98% breathing air. Examination is normal. She rates her pain 9 out of 10.
questions.q: How is the painful crisis best diagnosed?
o: Clinically, from the history and examination
questions.e: Acute painful vaso-occlusive crises are diagnosed clinically; analgesia should not wait for tests.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.

clues: typical of her usual painful crises
steps.x: A typical crisis with no red flags.

elim: Not needed to diagnose an acute painful crisis.
Confirms sickle cell disease, which is already known.
Not indicated for a typical crisis with normal examination.
There is no blood test that confirms a painful crisis.

steps.x: **B. Clinically, from the history and examination.** Vaso-occlusive crisis is a clinical diagnosis; treat the pain early.

questions.stem: A 40 year old woman with sickle cell disease has had a deep ache in her right shoulder for 3 months. It is worse when she raises her arm and is now disturbing her sleep. She has no fever or injury. Active and passive abduction are painful. A shoulder X-ray is normal.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate next investigation?
questions.e: MRI detects avascular necrosis early, before X-ray changes appear; the humeral head is a common site after the femoral head.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.
Suspected avascular necrosis with a normal X-ray.

elim: Does not image the humeral head marrow.
No fever or effusion to suggest septic arthritis.
No neurological symptoms.
Waiting delays diagnosis; early avascular necrosis is X-ray negative.

steps.x: **C. MRI of the right shoulder.** Suspected avascular necrosis with a normal X-ray: MRI.

questions.stem: A 19 year old man with sickle cell disease was admitted yesterday with a painful crisis affecting his ribs and back. He now has a cough and a temperature of 38.1°C. His respiratory rate is 26 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. There are crackles at the left base.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Suspected acute chest syndrome is confirmed by new pulmonary infiltrates on chest X-ray.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.

clues: admitted yesterday with a painful crisis
steps.x: Fever, hypoxia and basal crackles during a crisis.

elim: Not first line; the picture fits acute chest syndrome, confirmed by a new infiltrate.
Nonspecific and usually raised in a crisis.
Does not show pulmonary infiltrates.
Does not help in an acutely hypoxic patient.

steps.x: **A. Chest X-ray.** Suspected acute chest syndrome: chest X-ray looking for a new infiltrate.

questions.stem: A 17 year old girl with sickle cell disease has had three episodes of colicky right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals over 2 months. Each lasted about 2 hours and settled. She is well today with no fever. She has mild scleral icterus, which is usual for her. Abdominal examination is normal.

visual.title: Where the pain was
visual.caption: Episodic right upper quadrant pain after meals.

questions.q: Which is the most appropriate initial investigation?
questions.e: Chronic haemolysis causes pigment gallstones; biliary colic is investigated first with abdominal ultrasound.

steps.x: An investigation question: decide what the test must show and when it fits in the pathway.

clues: colicky right upper quadrant pain after fatty meals
scleral icterus, which is usual for her
steps.x: Biliary colic on a background of chronic haemolysis.

elim: Most gallstones are not seen on plain film.
Higher radiation and less sensitive than ultrasound for gallstones.
Invasive; for removing duct stones, not first-line diagnosis.
Assesses the stomach and duodenum, not the gallbladder.

steps.x: **A. Abdominal ultrasound.** Sickle cell + biliary colic: think pigment stones, scan with ultrasound.

questions.stem: A 26 year old man with sickle cell disease arrives at the Emergency Department with a painful crisis in his legs for 5 hours. He took paracetamol and ibuprofen at home with no relief. He scores his pain 9 out of 10. His observations are normal. Blood tests have been sent.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Oral codeine and review in 2 hours
Strong opioid such as morphine within 30 minutes
questions.e: NICE NG143: offer analgesia within 30 minutes of arrival; severe pain needs a strong opioid such as morphine, given early and aggressively.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Severe pain after failed home analgesia.

elim: Pain control must be early; the crisis is a clinical diagnosis.
Pethidine is not recommended in sickle cell crises.
Too weak and too slow for severe pain that home analgesia has not helped.
He has already failed this.

steps.x: **E. Strong opioid such as morphine within 30 minutes.** Vaso-occlusive crisis: early, aggressive analgesia with morphine (NICE NG143), plus fluids.

questions.stem: A 9 year old girl with sickle cell disease has a painful crisis in her arms. She has been given IV morphine and IV fluids. Her temperature is 39.1°C, pulse rate 130 bpm, BP 96/58 mmHg and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air. Her chest is clear. She has missed her penicillin for a week. Blood cultures have been taken.
questions.q: Which is the next most appropriate step in management?
o: Restart oral penicillin and review tomorrow
questions.e: Fever in a hyposplenic child off prophylaxis may be sepsis with an encapsulated organism; treat the trigger urgently with IV antibiotics.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: missed her penicillin for a week
steps.x: Febrile, tachycardic, hyposplenic child.

elim: Not indicated; there is no stroke, acute chest syndrome or organ failure.
A long-term preventive drug, not acute treatment.
Prophylactic doses do not treat possible sepsis in a hyposplenic child.
Not a treatment for fever; she is already functionally asplenic.

steps.x: **A. Broad-spectrum IV antibiotics.** Sickle crisis: analgesia, oxygen if hypoxic, fluids, and treat the trigger; fever = IV antibiotics.

questions.stem: A 5 year old boy with sickle cell disease has aplastic crisis confirmed by parvovirus B19 serology. He is pale and tachycardic but alert. His pulse rate is 144 bpm and BP 92/56 mmHg. Investigations: Hb 39 g/L (110–140; his baseline 78), reticulocytes 0.1% (0.5–2.5).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Aplastic crisis is self-limiting but the Hb can fall dangerously low; a simple top-up transfusion supports him until the marrow recovers.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Severe anaemia with no marrow response.

elim: Too slow; he needs red cells now.
Reserved for stroke, acute chest syndrome with hypoxia or multi-organ failure.
Not the first treatment for an aplastic crisis in sickle cell disease.
A long-term supplement; it will not correct an acute fall to 39 g/L.

steps.x: **E. Simple blood transfusion.** Sickle crisis with a low Hb: transfuse. Aplastic crisis: simple transfusion.

questions.stem: A 19 year old woman with sickle cell disease phones her GP. She has had severe pain in her back and legs for 12 hours that is not relieved by regular codeine and paracetamol at home. She has a temperature of 38.0°C. She lives alone and has vomited twice.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
o: Double the codeine dose and review in 48 hours
questions.e: An acute crisis not controlled by home analgesia, especially with fever and vomiting, needs urgent admission for IV morphine, IV fluids and treatment of the trigger.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: not relieved by regular codeine and paracetamol at home
steps.x: Uncontrolled pain, fever and vomiting.

elim: Leaves uncontrolled pain, fever and vomiting at home.
Undertreats a febrile crisis that needs IV analgesia and fluids.
Far too slow for an acute crisis.
Preventive, not acute treatment.

steps.x: **E. Urgent admission to hospital.** Acute sickle crisis that home analgesia does not control: admit urgently.

questions.stem: A 23 year old man with sickle cell disease has acute chest syndrome. His temperature is 38.6°C, respiratory rate 28 breaths per minute and oxygen saturation 92% breathing air. Chest X-ray shows right lower zone consolidation. He has been given high-flow oxygen and IV morphine. Blood for cross-match has been sent.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic treatment?
questions.e: First step in acute chest syndrome: high-flow oxygen, analgesia, antibiotics WITH atypical cover (a cephalosporin plus a macrolide) and simple transfusion.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Infection is a common cause of acute chest syndrome, including atypical organisms.

elim: Lacks the atypical cover that acute chest syndrome needs.
Gram-positive cover only, with no atypical cover.
Too narrow and lacks atypical cover in a hypoxic patient.
A urinary antibiotic.

steps.x: **B. IV cefotaxime and oral clarithromycin.** Acute chest syndrome antibiotics must include atypical cover.

questions.stem: An 8 year old girl with sickle cell disease has sudden left-sided weakness and slurred speech. CT head shows no haemorrhage and MRI confirms an acute right middle cerebral artery infarct. Her capillary glucose is 6.1 mmol/L and oxygen saturation 97% breathing air.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate management?
questions.e: Exchange transfusion rapidly lowers the HbS percentage and is indicated for stroke in sickle cell disease.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: acute right middle cerebral artery infarct
8 year old girl with sickle cell disease
steps.x: Acute ischaemic stroke caused by sickling.

elim: Does not reduce HbS, which is the cause of the stroke.
Too slow to act in an acute stroke.
Not the standard treatment for stroke in children with sickle cell disease.
The stroke is from sickling, not a venous clot.

steps.x: **B. Exchange transfusion.** Exchange transfusion: stroke, severe acute chest syndrome, multi-organ failure, rapid Hb fall.

questions.stem: A 16 year old boy with sickle cell disease is seen in clinic after his second admission with acute chest syndrome in 9 months, one of which needed exchange transfusion. Between episodes he is well. He takes folic acid and is up to date with vaccinations.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate long-term treatment to reduce further episodes?
questions.e: Hydroxycarbamide is used long-term after acute chest syndrome as well as for recurrent painful crises; it raises HbF and reduces sickling.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.

clues: second admission with acute chest syndrome in 9 months
steps.x: Recurrent acute chest syndrome.

elim: Does not prevent sickling and has major side effects.
An asthma treatment; does not reduce sickling.
Does not prevent acute chest syndrome; he is already functionally asplenic.
Acute chest syndrome is not a thromboembolic disease.

steps.x: **A. Hydroxycarbamide.** Recurrent acute chest syndrome or >3 painful crises a year: hydroxycarbamide.

questions.stem: A 31 year old woman with sickle cell disease attends her annual review in October. She had her pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine 2 years ago and takes folic acid daily. She is well with no crises this year. She asks which vaccine she should have now.
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate vaccine to offer today?
questions.e: Prevention in sickle cell disease includes an annual influenza vaccine, pneumococcal polysaccharide vaccine every 5 years and folic acid.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
Pneumococcal is not due; the yearly vaccine is.

elim: Not routinely given to adults in the UK and not specific to sickle cell disease.
A travel vaccine; she is not travelling.
Repeated every 5 years; she had it 2 years ago.
Offered at older ages in the UK.

steps.x: **B. Influenza vaccine.** Sickle cell prevention: annual flu vaccine, pneumococcal every 5 years, folic acid, penicillin in children.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy with sickle cell disease is seen in the haematology clinic. He takes twice daily phenoxymethylpenicillin and his vaccinations are up to date. His parents ask if he needs any other regular medication. His Hb is 78 g/L (his usual) and reticulocytes 10% (0.5–2.5).
questions.q: Which is the most appropriate additional regular medication?
questions.e: Chronic haemolysis with a brisk reticulocyte response uses up folate, so regular folic acid is part of standard prevention.

steps.x: A management question: decide where the patient is in the pathway and what comes next.
High red cell turnover raises folate demand.

elim: Iron is not deficient; haemolysis does not cause iron loss and transfusions can overload.
For recurrent crises; he has had none described.
Not used for sickle cell disease.
He has no B12 deficiency.

steps.x: **B. Folic acid.** Long-term sickle care: penicillin (children), vaccines, folic acid, specialist follow-up.

questions.stem: A 4 year old girl is diagnosed with sickle cell disease after newborn screening was missed. Her parents ask what has gone wrong in her blood. Haemoglobin electrophoresis shows HbS with no HbA. Her red cells take on a sickle shape when deoxygenated.
questions.q: Which is the most likely molecular cause?
o: Point mutation in the beta-globin gene
questions.e: A single point mutation in the beta-globin gene (glutamate to valine) produces haemoglobin S.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding from the mechanism, not just name the condition.
An abnormal haemoglobin, not reduced amounts of normal haemoglobin.

elim: Causes alpha-thalassaemia.
Causes hereditary spherocytosis.
Causes beta-thalassaemia, not HbS.
Causes conditions such as Huntington's disease.

steps.x: **C. Point mutation in the beta-globin gene.** Sickle cell disease = point mutation in beta-globin making HbS.

questions.stem: A 28 year old man with sickle cell disease goes trekking at high altitude in Nepal. On day 3 he develops severe pain in his back and legs. He has been drinking well and the weather is mild. His oxygen saturation is 88% breathing air at the lodge.
questions.q: Which best explains why his crisis started?
o: Altitude causes an autoimmune attack on red cells
Cold denatures HbA into Heinz bodies
Deoxygenated HbS polymerises and distorts red cells
Low oxygen activates platelets to form clots
questions.e: HbS polymerises when deoxygenated, making rigid sickle cells that raise viscosity and block small vessels, causing a vaso-occlusive crisis.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding from the mechanism, not just name the condition.
Hypoxia is the trigger here.

elim: Sickling is not immune-mediated.
Heinz bodies are a G6PD feature, and the weather is mild.
Hypoxia does not reduce HbS; it makes HbS polymerise.
Vaso-occlusion is from rigid sickled red cells, not platelet thrombosis.

steps.x: **C. Deoxygenated HbS polymerises and distorts red cells.** Hypoxia, dehydration, acidosis and cold make HbS polymerise and cells sickle.

questions.stem: A 20 year old woman with sickle cell disease has a painful crisis in her thigh bones after a long day without drinking. Examination is normal and her Hb is at her baseline. She asks why the pain is so severe when nothing looks wrong.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her pain?
o: Compression of nerves by an enlarged spleen
Microvascular occlusion causing bone ischaemia and infarction
questions.e: Sickled cells obstruct small vessels, causing tissue ischaemia, infarction and pain.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding from the mechanism, not just name the condition.
Dehydration trigger, normal examination, stable Hb.

elim: Sickle crises are not haemorrhagic.
The spleen is not involved in bone pain.
That describes reactive or immune arthritis.
Haemolysis causes jaundice, not bone pain; her Hb is stable.

steps.x: **D. Microvascular occlusion causing bone ischaemia and infarction.** Vaso-occlusion → ischaemia → infarction → pain.

questions.stem: A 24 year old woman with sickle cell disease has a laparoscopic cholecystectomy for recurrent biliary colic. The pathology report describes multiple small, dark, hard gallstones. Before surgery her bilirubin was 52 µmol/L (<21), mostly unconjugated, with normal ALT and ALP.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of her gallstones?
o: Bile duct infection with liver flukes
Excess unconjugated bilirubin from chronic haemolysis
Reduced bile salts from ileal disease
questions.e: Chronic haemolysis gives a raised unconjugated bilirubin, which precipitates as black pigment gallstones.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding from the mechanism, not just name the condition.
Dark stones with a raised unconjugated bilirubin.

elim: Causes brown stones in endemic areas; no exposure history.
She is not pregnant and stones would be cholesterol.
Produces pale cholesterol stones, not dark pigment stones.
Causes cholesterol stones, e.g. in Crohn's disease.

steps.x: **B. Excess unconjugated bilirubin from chronic haemolysis.** Chronic haemolysis → unconjugated bilirubin → pigment gallstones and jaundice.

questions.stem: A 22 year old man with sickle cell disease started daily oral hydroxycarbamide after four painful crises in a year. Six months later he has had no further admissions. His haemoglobin electrophoresis is repeated to assess his response.
questions.q: Which change is most likely on his repeat electrophoresis?
questions.e: Hydroxycarbamide increases fetal haemoglobin (HbF), which interferes with HbS polymerisation and reduces the frequency and severity of sickling.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding from the mechanism, not just name the condition.
The drug works by switching on fetal haemoglobin.

elim: He cannot make HbA without a normal beta-globin gene.
HbS is still produced; it is diluted, not removed.
The opposite of the drug's effect.
A marker of beta-thalassaemia trait, not the drug's effect.

steps.x: **E. Rise in HbF.** Hydroxycarbamide ↑ HbF → less HbS polymerisation → fewer crises.

questions.stem: A couple attend a genetics clinic. Their first child has sickle cell disease (HbSS). Both parents are well, and haemoglobin electrophoresis shows that each of them has both HbA and HbS. They are planning a second pregnancy and ask about the chance of another affected child.
questions.q: Which is the chance that their next child will have sickle cell disease?
questions.e: Sickle cell disease is autosomal recessive: two carriers have a 1 in 4 chance with each pregnancy of an affected child.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding from the mechanism, not just name the condition.

clues: each of them has both HbA and HbS
steps.x: Two healthy carriers of an autosomal recessive condition.

elim: The chance of a child being a carrier like the parents.
Not a recognised risk for two carriers.
The chance an unaffected sibling is a carrier.
Each pregnancy carries the same independent 1 in 4 risk.

steps.x: **B. 1 in 4.** Autosomal recessive, two carriers: 1 in 4 affected, 1 in 2 carriers, 1 in 4 unaffected.

questions.stem: A 3 year old boy with sickle cell disease is admitted with pneumococcal septicaemia. His parents ask why he is so prone to this infection. Abdominal ultrasound last year showed a small, scarred spleen. A blood film shows Howell-Jolly bodies.
questions.q: Which is the most likely mechanism of his increased risk of this infection?
o: Functional hyposplenism from repeated splenic infarction
questions.e: Repeated splenic infarction causes functional hyposplenism, so encapsulated organisms such as Streptococcus pneumoniae are poorly cleared.

steps.x: A science question: explain the finding from the mechanism, not just name the condition.
Evidence of loss of splenic function.

elim: HbS is not linked to complement genes.
Haemolysis does not lower antibody levels.
His marrow is overactive, not suppressed.
The thymus is not affected.

steps.x: **B. Functional hyposplenism from repeated splenic infarction.** Splenic infarction → functional asplenia → encapsulated organism infection.
